text: Given a string s and a dictionary, wordDict, return true if s can be segmented into a sequence of one or more dictionary words. Words may be reused.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the whole string must be covered with no leftover characters, words can repeat, and I only need a yes or no?
Right. Length up to three hundred, dictionary up to a thousand words.

Got it. Let me run through an example. Leetcode, with the dictionary leet and code, splits as leet, code, so true. And cats and og, with cat, cats, and, sand, and dog, can't be fully covered, so false.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. This problem reminds me of sequence-segmentation DP: dp of i means the first i characters can be segmented. dp of i is true if some word ends at i and the prefix before it, dp of i minus L, is already true. The subtle part is loop order. The position must be the outer loop, ascending, so that when I compute dp of i, every smaller dp of j is finalized. If I loop words on the outside instead, a word landing at i may need a dp of j that only a later word turns true — and I've already passed i. That version's answer even changes with dictionary order.

Here's the plan. One: dp of zero is true — the empty prefix. Two: for each position i, in ascending order, try every word; if it fits, the prefix before it is true, and the substring matches, mark dp of i true. Three: return dp of n. One thing worth flagging — the outer loop is the position, not the word. That's what guarantees all shorter prefixes are done before I use them. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it, and a variant if you have one.

Position outer, word inner. For each end position i, I try every word that could end there: it has to fit, the prefix before it has to be true, and the substring has to match. The line that matters is the outer loop header — position outside, ascending, so every shorter prefix is final before I read it. And a variant that scales better when the dictionary is large: put the words in a hash set and iterate cut points. Both keep the position on the outside. One thing worth flagging — the second one tries each cut point j and looks up the substring, so a position costs at most i lookups instead of a thousand word checks, and it breaks as soon as one split works.

Let's dry-run on the interleaving case: apple pen apple, with the dictionary apple and pen — expected true. The row that matters is thirteen. dp of thirteen leans on dp of eight, which position-outer finished at i equals eight, before reaching thirteen. A word-outer loop would test thirteen while dp of eight is still false, and wrongly answer false. That's the whole trap. Here it returns true. That matches.

Time is n times k times L for the word scan — k words, each up to L long. For the cut-point version there are n squared cut pairs, but each substring can be up to n characters to build and hash, so as written it's cubic in the worst case; capping the cut at the longest word brings it down to n times L squared. Space is linear. Oh, one more thing — the rule I'd carry away: sequence-segmentation problems want the position outside, because the pieces sit at fixed, interleaving spots; knapsack problems want the item outside, because you pick an unordered multiset. Same one-dimensional array, opposite outer loop.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You nailed why the position must be the outer loop, and that a word-outer loop is order-dependent and wrong. You gave the hash-set cut-point variant for large dictionaries. And you generalized the position-versus-item rule across DP families. Good work.
